content: Respiratory disease is a broad term that encompasses conditions affecting the lungs, pleural cavity, bronchial tubes, trachea, upper respiratory tract, as well as the nerves and muscles involved in breathing. These diseases can range in severity from mild and self-limiting conditions, such as the common cold, to severe and life-threatening illnesses, such as bacterial pneumonia or pulmonary embolism. In Canada, respiratory diseases account for over 10% of hospitalizations and more than 16% of deaths. The medical field dedicated to the study of respiratory diseases is known as pulmonology. Physicians who specialize in diagnosing and treating respiratory diseases are referred to as pulmonologists, chest medicine specialists, respiratory medicine specialists, respirologists, or thoracic medicine specialists. Certain respiratory conditions, such as pulmonary fibrosis, lead to a reduction in the functional volume of the lungs. Respiratory diseases can be further categorized into upper or lower respiratory tract diseases, a classification often used in the context of infectious respiratory illnesses. Additionally, they can be classified as parenchymal or vascular lung diseases. In terms of epidemiology, individuals in the United States experience approximately 1 billion cases of the common cold annually. In the United Kingdom, one in seven people is affected by some form of chronic lung disease, with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma being the most prevalent conditions.
